subject: Science
title: Year 9 Science Exam 9
topic: Electricity and magnetism · Mains electricity, power, magnets and electromagnets · AQA Higher
intro: You may use a calculator. For longer answers write in full sentences and use key words. Describe = say what happens; Explain = say what happens and why (use because and so). 6-mark questions are marked on how well your ideas link together: plan for a minute, then write about 6 linked points. Show your working for calculations and give units. Equations: P = V × I; P = I² × R; E = P × t; Q = I × t; V = I × R; F = B × I × l. Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40. Questions 16 to 18 go back over earlier units.

questions.q: What is the frequency of the UK mains electricity supply?
questions.ms: B1: 50 Hz. UK mains is 230 V alternating current at 50 Hz.

questions.q: What colour is the insulation on the live wire in a three-core cable?
questions.ms: B1: brown. Neutral is blue; earth is green and yellow stripes.

questions.q: What is the difference between alternating current (ac) and direct current (dc)?
options: ac keeps changing direction; dc flows in one direction only
dc keeps changing direction; ac flows in one direction only
ac is always a smaller current than dc
questions.ms: B1: ac repeatedly changes direction; dc (from a cell or battery) flows one way only.

questions.q: Which of these is a magnetic material?
questions.ms: B1: steel. The magnetic materials are iron, steel, cobalt and nickel.

questions.q: A steel paperclip is placed near a bar magnet and becomes an induced magnet. What force is there between them?
options: Attraction or repulsion, depending on the pole
questions.ms: B1: always attraction. An induced magnet always attracts the magnet that induced it.

questions.q: Which way do magnetic field lines point outside a bar magnet?
options: From the south pole to the north pole
From the north pole to the south pole
Round in circles about the middle of the magnet
questions.ms: B1: from north to south. A plotting compass points along the field lines, away from N and towards S.

questions.q:
A lamp is switched off, but the live wire is still connected to the lamp holder.
Explain why a person who touches the live wire can still get an electric shock.
questions.ms: B1: the live wire is still at a high potential (about 230 V) even when the switch is open. B1: the person's body is at 0 V (earth), so there is a large potential difference across the body and a current flows through it to earth.

questions.q:
A kettle has a metal case. A fault makes the live wire touch the case.
Explain how the earth wire and the fuse protect the user.
questions.ms: B1: the earth wire connects the case to earth / gives a low-resistance path, so the current flows through the earth wire (not the person). B1: a very large current flows. B1: the fuse melts / blows and breaks the circuit, so the case is no longer live (cuts off the live wire).

questions.q:
A kettle is connected to the 230 V mains. The current through it is 10 A.
Calculate the power of the kettle. (W)
questions.ms: Answer: 2300 W. M1 for P = 230 × 10. A1 for 2300 W (accept 2.3 kW).

questions.q:
The kettle is switched on for 3 minutes.
Calculate the energy transferred by the kettle. (J)
questions.ms: Answer: 414 000 J. B1 for 3 minutes = 180 s. M1 for E = 2300 × 180. A1 for 414 000 J. Follow through from 8a. Using t = 3 (6900 J): B0 M1 A0.

questions.q:
A current of 3 A flows through a heater with a resistance of 20 Ω.
Calculate the power of the heater. (W)
questions.ms: Answer: 180 W. M1 for P = 3² × 20 = 9 × 20. A1 for 180 W. Common mistake: 3 × 20 = 60 (forgot to square the current).

questions.q: In the National Grid, what does a step-up transformer do?
options: Increases the potential difference and decreases the current
Increases both the potential difference and the current
Decreases the potential difference and increases the current
questions.ms: B1: it increases the potential difference (to hundreds of thousands of volts) and decreases the current, so the power stays the same.

questions.q: Explain why electricity is sent through the National Grid cables at a very high potential difference.
questions.ms: B1: a high potential difference means a low current (for the same power, P = VI). B1: a lower current means less heating of the cables (P = I²R). B1: so less energy is wasted / lost to the surroundings, which makes the National Grid more efficient.

questions.q: Describe how to use a plotting compass to show the shape of the magnetic field around a bar magnet, and describe the pattern you would see.
questions.ms: B1: put the magnet on paper and place the compass near one pole; mark the direction the needle points with dots at both ends. B1: move the compass so its tail is on the last dot, mark again, and repeat until you reach the other pole; join the dots to make a field line, then repeat from different starting points. B1: the lines go from the north pole round to the south pole (draw arrows N to S). B1: the lines are closest together at the poles, where the field is strongest.

questions.q: Describe the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.
questions.ms: B1: a permanent magnet makes its own magnetic field all the time. B1: an induced magnet only becomes a magnet when it is in a magnetic field, and loses most or all of its magnetism when taken out of the field.

questions.q: A current flows through a long straight wire. Describe the magnetic field around the wire.
questions.ms: B1: the field lines are circles around the wire (concentric circles). B1: the field is strongest close to the wire / gets weaker further away; reversing the current reverses the direction of the field. (Any 2.)

questions.q:
A student makes an electromagnet by winding a coil of wire around an iron nail. She counts how many paperclips it picks up for different numbers of turns.
Number of turnsTrial 1Trial 2Trial 3Mean
103423
206756
3091089
4012412X
5015161415

One result in the row for 40 turns is anomalous. Which one?
questions.ms: Answer: trial 2. B1. 4 paperclips is far below the other two (12 and 12) and does not fit the pattern.

questions.q: Calculate the mean number of paperclips X for 40 turns, ignoring the anomaly.
questions.ms: Answer: 12. B1 for (12 + 12) ÷ 2 = 12. Including the anomaly (9.3): 0.

questions.q: Describe the relationship between the number of turns and the number of paperclips picked up. Use data from the table.
questions.ms: B1: as the number of turns increases, the number of paperclips increases. B1: they are directly proportional / every extra 10 turns picks up 3 more paperclips, e.g. 10 turns picks up 3 and 20 turns picks up 6 (doubling the turns doubles the paperclips).

questions.q: Give two control variables for this investigation.
questions.ms: B1 each, any two: the current / potential difference of the power supply; the same type and size of iron core (nail); the same size and type of paperclips; the same wire.

questions.q:
A scrapyard crane uses a large electromagnet to lift old cars and drop them into a crusher.
Explain how the electromagnet works, why an electromagnet is used instead of a permanent magnet, and how the electromagnet could be made stronger.
questions.ms: 6 marks, level-marked. Level 3 (5-6 marks): a detailed, logically linked answer covering most points. Level 2 (3-4 marks): several relevant points, some linked. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, separate statements. Indicative content: a current flows through a coil of wire (solenoid); this makes a magnetic field around the coil; the coil is wound around an iron core; the iron core becomes an induced magnet and makes the field much stronger; car bodies are made of steel, which is a magnetic material, so they are attracted; an electromagnet can be switched off: when the current is switched off the field disappears (iron is magnetically soft / loses its magnetism) and the car is dropped over the crusher; a permanent magnet cannot be switched off, so it could not let go of the car; stronger: increase the current, increase the number of turns on the coil, use an iron core (or a larger one) / put the turns closer together.

questions.q:
Higher. A wire carrying a current of 3 A is placed at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.2 T. The length of wire in the field is 0.5 m.
Calculate the force on the wire. (N)
questions.ms: Answer: 0.3 N. M1 for F = 0.2 × 3 × 0.5. A1 for 0.3 N.

questions.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the first finger point in the direction of?
questions.ms: B1: the magnetic field (First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion).

questions.q:
Describe how a student could investigate how the current through a coil affects the strength of an electromagnet.
Include the equipment, how to measure the strength, how to make it a fair test, and how to use the results.
questions.ms: 6 marks, level-marked (investigative skills). Level 3 (5-6 marks): a detailed, logically linked answer covering most points. Level 2 (3-4 marks): several relevant points, some linked. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, separate statements. Indicative content: wind a coil of insulated wire around an iron nail / core; connect it in series with a power supply, a variable resistor (rheostat) and an ammeter; use the variable resistor to set the current, e.g. 0.5 A, 1.0 A, 1.5 A, 2.0 A, 2.5 A; measure strength by counting the paperclips picked up (or the distance at which a compass needle moves, or a mass on a balance); repeat each current three times and work out a mean, ignoring anomalies; control variables: same number of turns, same core, same size paperclips, same wire; switch off between readings because the wire gets hot (safety, and heating changes the resistance); plot a line graph of current (x-axis) against number of paperclips (y-axis) and describe the pattern: a bigger current makes a stronger electromagnet.

questions.q:
Revisit (circuits). A 5 Ω resistor and a 15 Ω resistor are connected in series with a 6 V battery.
Calculate the current in the circuit. (A)
questions.ms: Answer: 0.3 A. M1 for total resistance 5 + 15 = 20 Ω and I = 6 ÷ 20. A1 for 0.3 A.

questions.q: Calculate the potential difference across the 15 Ω resistor. (V)
questions.ms: Answer: 4.5 V. M1 for V = 0.3 × 15. A1 for 4.5 V. (The 5 Ω resistor gets the other 1.5 V.)

questions.q:
Revisit (charge). A current of 0.4 A flows through a motor for 5 minutes.
Calculate the charge that flows through the motor. (C)
questions.ms: Answer: 120 C. B1 for 5 minutes = 300 s. M1 for Q = 0.4 × 300. A1 for 120 C. Using t = 5 (2 C): B0 M1 A0.

questions.q:
Revisit (reacting masses). When calcium carbonate is heated it breaks down: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
Calculate the maximum mass of calcium oxide (CaO) that can be made from 50 g of calcium carbonate. (g)
questions.ms: Answer: 28 g. M1 for Mr of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 100. M1 for Mr of CaO = 40 + 16 = 56 (ratio 1 : 1, so 100 g → 56 g). A1 for 50 × 56/100 = 28 g.

questions.q: A student only collects 21 g of calcium oxide. Calculate the percentage yield. (%)
questions.ms: Answer: 75%. M1 for 21 ÷ 28 × 100. A1 for 75%. Follow through from 18a.

questions.q: Give two reasons why the actual yield is less than the maximum.
questions.ms: B1 each, any two: the reaction was not complete (not all of the calcium carbonate broke down); some product was lost, e.g. left in the container or spilt when transferring; the calcium carbonate was not pure; some of the product reacted in a different way / with something else.
